project.title: Sorting algorithms, measured
project.alt: Actual sorting trace with original-position markers and exact evidence of equal items changing relative order
project.desc: Track original items through sorting exchanges and inspect equal-value order, while keeping operation counts separate from runtime.
project.built: Extended the existing traces with immutable original item identities, optional position labels and observed equal-value order evidence on the same shared input.
project.why: Equal numbers look interchangeable in a sorting animation. Original positions reveal relative-order changes and help distinguish one observed result from a general stability guarantee.
how: Choose repeated values or a custom input, then enable original positions. Each # identifies a starting item, independent of its value or current rank.
Step through actual exchanges and inspect the original/current order of repeated values. Compare observed final order for the same input across three traces.
Keep operation totals separate from the preserved five-algorithm Python benchmark; original implementations and recorded measurements remain unchanged.
project.demonstrates: Algorithmic reasoning, immutable trace state, controlled examples, regression testing and accessible interactive teaching.
project.caption: Genuine browser capture with original positions enabled. Equal-item order follows actual exchanges. Counts are JavaScript trace operations, not measured Python runtime.
project.result: Five Python implementations passed correctness checks on 125 measured sorts: five identical seeded random samples at each size from 50 to 1,000. Median and IQR are calculated from saved raw measurements. Measurements were recorded on Windows-11-10.0.26300-SP0 with Python 3.12.2; unchanged algorithm hashes reuse those observations. The browser explorer compares complete key-comparison/index-swap totals for three actual traces on the same generated or validated custom input. Selecting a trace and resetting preserve its starting values. These operation counts and animation pace are separate from the recorded Python runtime measurements.
project.limits: Measurements cover random non-negative integer inputs from 50 to 1,000 in one recorded environment; they do not establish a universal ranking. IQR describes observed variation, not confidence. Rightmost-pivot recursive quicksort has adverse-input recursion limits. Radix supports non-negative integers and rejects booleans/fractions. The browser explorer ports only three approaches and limits inputs to 24 values; animation pace is unrelated to Python runtime.
project.technical: Every frame copies original identities alongside values. Real index-changing exchanges swap both; self placements change neither. A pure helper validates the permutation and compares repeated-value subsequences with their original order. Labels are one-based, while toggling retains the step and input. Dense labelled charts have readable minimum-width bars and keyboard scrolling. Seven Python tests preserve algorithms/cache provenance; eight Node tests reconcile every frame identity/value, independent snapshots and known reversals. Five browser journeys cover exact identities, evidence, keyboard toggling/scrolling and mobile fit alongside existing playback/custom-input checks.
project.run: Install requirements.txt; run python benchmark_portfolio.py, python plot_portfolio.py and python -m unittest discover -p "test_*.py" -v. Use --refresh to request new measurements. For browser verification, build Python fixtures and docs, npm ci, npm run test:trace and npm run test:browser.
gallery: The same input across three traces, including observed equal-value order. Preserved once is not a proof of stability.
Original-position markers and exact repeated-value order on mobile; dense labelled charts scroll internally.
Preserved Python measurements remain a separate experiment with unchanged algorithm and data hashes.
project.demo_disclosure: Interactive browser explanation of three sorting approaches. Playback is illustrative; measured Python benchmarks are presented separately.
project.challenge: Sorted numbers cannot reveal whether equal items changed places. Original identities must follow every real exchange without changing comparisons, swap counts or historical frames. The evidence names the scope: preserving order on this input is not proof of general stability. Known selection-sort and rightmost-pivot quicksort counterexamples reveal reversals without altering algorithm behavior.
